(This evening through Thursday)...
Issued at 307 PM EST Thu Nov 26 2026

Rest of today through tonight...

Deep upper low centered over the TN valley will shift east then 
northeast into the upper OH valley. Strong WAA noted on ACARS 
soundings this afternoon will gradually wane as dynamic cooling 
takes over with the deformation zone shifting ewd from the MS 
valley into central Indiana overnight. Recent abatement of the 
heavier precip has allowed for the stronger low level jet winds 
(40 kts at 925 mb) to begin to mix down to the surface. Wind gusts
will remain between 30-35 kts across northern areas where a 
stronger low level jet is coupled with the strongest pressure 
gradient. These winds are expected to begin diminishing this 
evening as low levels begin to cool and core of the low level jet 
shifts northeast into Ohio ahead of the dynamic low level cooling.

Ptype will remain rain through late evening as temperatures 
gradually fall at the surface to between 37 and 39 degrees. Forecast 
soundings from a consensus of model solutions show substantial 
cooling in the 925-700 mb layer occurring generally after 03Z (much 
sooner after 00Z on the GFS) with a ptype change over to a very wet 
snow and/or rain/snow mix most areas after 06Z. Recent observations 
in parts of middle TN with similar thermodynamic profiles to what is 
forecast for central Indiana late tonight indicate that temps will 
likely fall to around 34-35 degrees with light snow. Given warm 
ground temperatures, light snow intensity and surface temps above 
freezing there are no concerns for snow accumulations nor black ice 
development.  

Friday...

On the back side of the rapidly departing upper low, the deformation 
zone will shift eastward away from central Indiana by mid morning. 
Residual cyclonic flow coupled with moderately steep low level lapse 
rates will support residual scattered showers and gusty W-NW winds 
from 20-30 mph during late morning into mid afternoon. Increasing 
warm advection and larger scale subsidence will progressively end 
precip/erode clouds from the west during the mid-late afternoon. 

Friday night through Saturday night...

In the wake of the upper low, skies will clear out Friday evening. 
Scattered high clouds are expected to move over the area late Friday 
night lasting through most of Saturday associated with a weak 
shortwave trough passing through the region. Moderate WAA ushered in 
by low level SW winds will support temps increasing to near or 
slightly above seasonal norms, around 50 F, on Saturday despite 
partly cloudy skies. A stronger shortwave trough presently moving 
into BC Canada will shift eastward along the U.S Canadian border 
with additional shortwave energy rotating around a weak upper ridge 
over the SW states and into the central and southern Plains. These 
shortwaves will support a deepening area of surface low pressure 
along with increasing low-mid level frontogenetic forcing over the 
Plains on Saturday. These factors combined with increasing low level 
waa/moistening out ahead of this system will lead to the chance of 
light precip to move into central Indiana late Saturday night. 

Sunday and Sunday night...

A deepening area of low pressure aided by increasing moisture flux 
(PWATs 125% of normal) along with a 30-40 kt low level jet will 
support a band of moderate to potentially heavy rain ahead of an 
area of low pressure and attendant cold front moving across central 
Indiana on Sunday. Forecast soundings suggest little in the way of 
positive area, especially from surface based parcels, with a slight 
amount of elevated instability (MUCAPE around 80 J/KG) showing up in 
a zone of step mid level lapse rates in the mid level dry slot. 
Therefore, no thunder will be mentioned in the forecast for the time 
being. In the wake of the cold front, model consensus is that strong 
CAA will help shift ptype from light rain to light snow at the very 
end of the event in the deformation zone as thicknesses crash to 
near 535 dm. Given uncertainty this far out with such subtle timing 
and small chances along with marginal surface temperatures, will 
leave any mention of snow out of the forecast for now. What is more 
likely is fairly strong wind gusts give a strong pressure gradient 
and CAA enhancing low level lapse rates. Gusts up to 40 mph look 
possible Sunday evening before gradually weakening overnight.  

Monday through Wednesday....

Mainly zonal flow is expected in the wake of Sunday's storm. A broad 
area of surface high pressure will move from the plains into the 
Ohio Valley by Tuesday morning. Timing of lightest winds with 
morning lows seems a little off so min temps are not expected to 
fall as much as previously expected with most readings being the 
upper 20s both Monday and Tuesday morning. After recent rains, if 
winds become lighter than forecast areas of fog (potentially dense) 
will become a factor. WAA will commence Tuesday ahead another 
deepening area of surf
